design_detail: Dose-response meta-analysis of 34 prospective cohort studies (56 independent curves by sex, age group, beverage or ethnic group; 1,015,835 participants, 94,533 deaths) of alcohol intake and all-cause mortality published up to December 2005, found by one PubMed search and reference lists. Curves were pooled by inverse-variance-weighted second-order fractional-polynomial meta-regression allowing for correlation within studies (best fit: log RR = b1 x^0.5 + b2 x^0.5 log x), with fixed effects as the main model and a random-effects repeat; subgroups by adjustment level, sex, region, reference group, study size, follow-up and publication year with 99% confidence intervals and Sidak-adjusted contrasts. Reference: each study's lowest-intake category. No protocol, no appraisal of the included studies, no test for publication bias.
can_establish: The shape and size of the pooled association between alcohol intake and all-cause mortality in cohort studies published up to 2005, and how it changed with adjustment for confounders, sex, region, the composition of the reference group, follow-up and publication year.
cannot_establish: That drinking at low or moderate levels lowers mortality (pooled observational cohorts; residual confounding and reference-group bias not removed, and the inverse association was smaller and ended at lower intake when former and light drinkers were excluded from the reference group); the precision of the pooled curve (the tabulated intervals are fixed-effect despite large heterogeneity); or the completeness of the evidence (one database, no appraisal of the included studies, publication bias not assessed).

sample.recruitment: Review-level: PubMed, no start date, to December 2005 (humans; title or abstract containing alcohol, beer, wine or spirits plus mortality or death), and the references of the selected articles. 73 publications identified; excluded: one risk category only (4), mortality not reported separately by sex (5), cause-specific mortality only (3), multiple reports of one cohort (9; the longest follow-up kept), reference category not the lowest intake (4), relative risks or cases and person-years unavailable (14) (Methods › Search strategy and data extraction, 1st paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Prospective studies of alcohol dose and total mortality reporting at least two intake categories, by sex, with the lowest-intake category as reference and usable relative risks or counts; no language or population restriction is stated.
sample.demographics: Study level only (Table 1): cohorts from Japan, the United Kingdom, Denmark, Poland, Germany, Russia, the United States, Sweden, France, China, Australia and Italy, published 1981 to 2005; follow-up 5.5 to 26 years; age ranges at entry from 18 to 84 where given; 37 curves in men and 19 in women. Several cohorts are occupational or volunteer samples, according to the reference titles (male British doctors, male Japanese physicians, male German construction workers, the Physicians' Health Study enrolment cohort, men enrolled in an American Cancer Society study).
sample.attrition: Not applicable at review level; attrition in the primary cohorts is not reported.
sample.selection_effects: One database plus reference lists; no grey literature; excluded studies are given only as counts. The meta-analysis inherits each cohort's reference group: in 26 of 56 curves former drinkers were not excluded from it. Few cohorts adjusted for or excluded pre-existing disease (by Table 1's codes, 4 adjusted for baseline diseases and 4 for coronary disease).

exposure.measurement: Self-reported baseline intake as reported by each cohort, assigned in grams a day: the midpoint of each reported range, and 1.2 times the lower bound for open-ended top categories. A drink was taken as defined by each study; where undefined (7 studies) as 10 g of ethanol, and the authors say that 12 or 14 g gave the same results (data not shown) (Methods, p. 2439).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Curves plotted from 0 to 70 g a day; the figures' drinks-per-day axis equates one drink with 10 g, so the abstract's '1-2 drinks' and '2-4 drinks' are about 10 to 20 and 20 to 40 g a day (editors' conversion from the axes). Drinking pattern and beverage were not analysed, except one cohort reported for wine and beer separately.
exposure.polysubstance: Smoking adjusted in 27 of the 34 studies, by Table 1's codes; other drugs not addressed.

comparison.controls: Each cohort's lowest-intake category: no alcohol intake with former drinkers excluded (30 curves), declared no alcohol use (12) or occasional use (14), with former drinkers not excluded in either (Results › All studies, 1st paragraph). Among the 48 adjusted curves, 27 were classed as without and 21 as with light and/or former drinkers in the reference group (Table 2); whether the 27 also excluded occasional drinkers is not stated consistently (reporting issue 6).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Lifetime drinking history, reasons for not drinking and pre-existing illness are not available at review level; by Table 1's codes only 4 studies adjusted for baseline diseases.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Smoking of the reference groups not reported.

outcomes.instruments: All-cause mortality as reported by each cohort; adjusted relative risks extracted whenever possible, otherwise crude relative risks and 95% CIs computed from the number of events (5 studies) (Methods, p. 2439).
outcomes.validity_norms: Death ascertainment as in each cohort (not described).
outcomes.operationalization: 'Protection' is a pooled RR below 1 against the reference category; 'maximum protection' is 1 minus the lowest pooled RR; the 'reversion point' is the intake above which the inverse association is no longer significant at the 99% level (Table 2 footnote).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Partial: 99% confidence intervals in subgroup analyses and Sidak-adjusted pairwise contrasts (Methods › Data analysis); seven subgroup families were tested.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not reported; data acquisition is credited to two authors, without a statement on independent or duplicate extraction.

analysis.effect_sizes: All 56 curves (fixed effects): best fit b1 = -0.1592 (SE 0.0056), b2 = 0.0421 (SE 0.0014); lowest mortality at 6 g a day, RR 0.81 (95% CI 0.80 to 0.83), i.e. maximum protection 19% (95% CI 17 to 20); inverse association significant up to 42 g a day. Random effects: same model, very similar curve, wider intervals (Figure 1 only); deviance 879.4 (fixed) against 154.0 (random). Maximum protection (99% CI) at the intake of lowest risk, and reversion point (Table 2): not adjusted (8 curves) 36% (21 to 40) at 10 g, 68 g; adjusted at least for age (48) 17% (15 to 18) at 6 g, 37 g; also for social status (28) 18% (15 to 21) at 9 g, 46 g; also for social status and diet (10) 18% (12 to 24) at 6 g, 30 g; women (16) 18% (13 to 22) at 5 g, 18 g; men (32) 17% (15 to 19) at 6 g, 38 g; women by region: US 19% (13 to 24), Europe 20% (3 to 34), Australia, Japan and China 12% (0 to 23), P > .54; men: US 16% (14 to 19) at 4 g, 27 g; Europe 24% (20 to 28) at 9 g, 58 g; Australia, Japan and China 18% (13 to 23) at 6 g, 33 g; reference group with light or former drinkers (21) 23% (20 to 26) at 8 g, 52 g, without (27) 16% (14 to 18) at 5 g, 30 g, P < .001; small studies (26) 17% (15 to 22), large (22) 15% (10 to 20), P = .61; follow-up 10 years or less (22) 21% (18 to 25), more (26) 15% (13 to 27 as printed), P < .001; published 1981-1998 (25) 15% (13 to 18), 1999-2005 (23) 21% (18 to 24), P < .001. In the 34 curves with both crude and adjusted estimates: 19% (17 to 21) crude against 16% (14 to 18) adjusted. No I2, tau-squared or prediction interval; no absolute rates.
analysis.covariates: None at review level; adjusted estimates as reported by each cohort, with adjustment sets in Table 1 ranging from age alone to 10 variables; subgroup analyses by level of adjustment.
analysis.selective_reporting: Several analyses are reported as 'data not shown' (12- or 14-g drinks; men against women within the 13 populations with both; ethnicity within US data). The random-effects results appear only as a curve in Figure 1, while all tabulated estimates and intervals are from the fixed-effect model. No test for publication bias.
analysis.power: Not addressed; subgroups with few curves have wide intervals (women in Europe, 5 curves: 3 to 34%; other countries, 4 curves: 0 to 23%).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In cohorts published up to 2005, the pooled fixed-effect relative risk of death fell steeply from the reference category to its lowest point at 5 to 6 g a day (about half a 10-g drink; RR 0.81) and then rose, with the inverse association no longer significant above 42 g a day (37 g in adjusted curves; 18 g in women, 38 g in men). It was smaller and ended at lower intake when former and light drinkers were excluded from the reference group (16% at 5 g, significance lost at 30 g) than when they were included (23% at 8 g, lost at 52 g); it was larger in unadjusted curves (36%, different studies), in European than US men, in shorter follow-up and in more recent publications. Heterogeneity was large, and the random-effects intervals are wider than the tabulated ones.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and conclusion speak of 'protection' and of windows of intake that may confer a "net beneficial effect of moderate drinking" (abstract, p. 2437; similar wording in the conclusion, p. 2444); the Comment calls the 15 to 18% benefit of undoubted public health value and judges residual confounding very unlikely to change the picture substantially (p. 2442); the conclusion recommends that people who already drink low to moderate amounts regularly "should be encouraged to continue" (p. 2444). Gaps: (1) causal and advisory language from pooled observational cohorts; (2) the residual-confounding argument assumes unmeasured confounding no stronger than measured confounding and rests on the 34 curves with both crude and adjusted estimates, an assumption that cannot be tested; (3) the reference-group result, which the Comment itself calls important, is absent from the abstract and the conclusion, although it moves the reversion point from 52 to 30 g a day; (4) the abstract's windows (1 to 2 drinks for women, 2 to 4 for men, in 10-g drinks) lie where the fitted curves are returning towards 1, not where mortality was lowest (editors' calculation: men 0.88 to 0.99 at 20 to 40 g a day, women 0.86 to 0.95 at 10 to 20 g), and the abstract's limit of 4 drinks a day in men differs from the limit of 3 given in the Results; (5) most of the fitted reduction lies between the reference category and the first grams of intake (RR 0.85 at 1 g a day, editors' calculation), the contrast most exposed to reference-group bias; (6) the tabulated intervals are fixed-effect and understate uncertainty; (7) publication bias is dismissed by argument, not tested.

timeline.event: White, Altmann and Nanchahal (BMJ), described here as a meta-analysis finding a J-shaped relation only in men over 34 and women over 54 (ref. 9).
Gmel, Gutjahr and Rehm: precision-weighted hierarchical meta-analysis of the alcohol and all-cause mortality curve (ref. 10).
Bagnardi et al.: the flexible meta-regression method used here, co-developed by the third author (ref. 11).
This meta-analysis (accepted 30 August 2006; issue of 11/25 December 2006).
Fillmore et al.: meta-analysis grouping studies by abstainer definition (Addiction Research and Theory; cited by Stockwell et al., 2024, not read).

Stockwell et al.: 87-study meta-analysis with lifetime-abstainer and bias-adjusted analyses, which according to its card does not cite this paper; the project list presents items 5 to 7 as critiques of it (card sc_stockwell_2016, this round).
Wood et al.: individual-participant analysis restricted to current drinkers, avoiding the abstainer reference group (card sc_wood_2018, this round).
Di Castelnuovo et al.: MORGAM analysis of 142,960 individuals by the same first author, one of the 20 cohorts added in Zhao et al. (2023) and Stockwell et al. (2024) (title as cited there; not read).
Zhao et al.: 107-cohort meta-analysis with study-level adjustment for abstainer biases (card sc_zhao_2023, this round).

Stockwell et al.: in the 6 cohorts recruited at a median age of 55 or younger with lifetime-abstainer references, low-volume RR 0.98 (0.87 to 1.11), against 0.84 in older cohorts with both abstainer biases (card sc_stockwell_2024, this round).

replication.where_it_stands: The standard citation for the J-shaped all-cause mortality curve in cohorts published up to 2005. Its own subgroup analysis anticipated the later critique: excluding former and light drinkers from the reference group reduced the inverse association and moved its end from 52 to 30 g a day. Later meta-analyses with stricter reference groups (Stockwell et al., 2016; Zhao et al., 2023; Stockwell et al., 2024, one group with overlapping data) found no significant reduction in the least-biased subgroups, and the Mendelian randomization studies carded in this round test the question differently. Claims may cite this paper for what the pre-2006 cohort literature showed and for how sensitive the curve was to the reference group, not for a protective effect of drinking.

funding.funder: Italian Ministry of University, Research, Education (MIUR), Decreto No. 1588-19/11/2004; the sponsor had no involvement in study design, data collection, analysis or interpretation, writing, or the decision to submit (Role of the Sponsor, p. 2444).
funding.affiliations_note: Laboratory of Genetic and Environmental Epidemiology, 'John Paul II' Center for High Technology Research and Education in Biomedical Sciences, Catholic University, Campobasso (five authors); Department of Statistics, University of Milan-Bicocca (Bagnardi, co-developer of the pooling method, ref. 11). The group's earlier papers on wine, beer and vascular risk and on alcohol and coronary heart disease are cited (refs 3, 7 and 12). Recorded as flags for closer reading, not as reasons to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: A pooled individual-participant analysis of cohorts with lifetime drinking histories, using lifetime abstainers and stable occasional drinkers as separate references, excluding or modelling baseline illness, reporting random-effects intervals and absolute death rates; together with genetic analyses able to estimate risk at low intake, which test the question without an abstainer reference group.

No protocol or registration is mentioned.
The Comment explains reliance on observational studies because controlled trials of alcohol are difficult and ethically questionable (p. 2443).
One database (PubMed) with the terms printed, plus reference lists; no second database, grey literature or registries; language limits not stated.
Not reported; data acquisition is credited to two authors without saying how extraction was done.

domains.note: Exclusions are given only as counts by reason (4, 5, 3, 9, 4 and 14).

domains.note: Table 1 gives country, follow-up, age range, participants, deaths, adjustment set and sex for each study; the reference category, intake measure and categories of each study are not given.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: No appraisal tool, but studies were classed by confounder adjustment (age, social status, diet) and by whether light or former drinkers were in the reference group, which touch confounding and selection; exposure measurement, baseline illness, attrition and selective reporting were not assessed.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported

domains.note: The dose-response method is appropriate in itself (weighted, allowing for correlation within studies), and adjusted estimates were preferred, but every tabulated estimate and interval comes from the fixed-effect model although the authors found substantial heterogeneity (deviance 879.4 against 154.0 with random effects); random-effects results appear only as a curve, and the main analysis mixes crude and adjusted curves.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: Subgroup analyses by level of adjustment and by composition of the reference group, and a same-study comparison of crude and adjusted estimates.

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: The Comment discusses residual confounding, the reference group and under-reporting of intake; it judges their impact small, which is the subject of the interpretation gap rather than a failure to discuss them.
Heterogeneity is shown by the deviances and explored by sex, region, reference group, size, follow-up and publication year, with the US-Europe difference in men discussed.
No funnel plot or test; dismissed by argument (Comment, p. 2443).

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Funding, the sponsor's role and a financial disclosure statement are printed.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Five critical items are 'no' (2, 4, 7, 11 and 15), so AMSTAR 2 gives critically low confidence. The judgment concerns how far the pooled numbers can be trusted as unbiased summaries: a single-database search, no appraisal of the cohorts, fixed-effect intervals despite large heterogeneity and no check for publication bias. The paper remains useful for what it shows about its own inputs: the J-shape in the pre-2006 cohort literature and its sensitivity to the reference group, to adjustment and to region. It may be cited for those descriptive points, attributed to the cohorts it pooled, and not for a causal effect or for the recommendation to keep drinking.

key_findings.finding: Publication bias was not assessed statistically: the authors argue that high-quality follow-up studies of total mortality are unlikely to have gone unpublished for negative results, so any bias would be weak. They add that under-reporting of intake would bias relative risks towards the null and may distort the shape of the J-curve and the apparent threshold for harm, and that controlled trials of alcohol are difficult and ethically questionable.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2's maximum-protection values for small (17%, 99% CI 15 to 22) and large studies (15%, 10 to 20) do not match Table 3's parameters, which give about 14% for small and 17% for large studies (editors' calculation), nor Figure 4B, in which the small-study curve is the shallower one (lowest RR about 0.85) with the wider interval; the reversion points (26 and 36 g) do match the figure. Smaller mismatches: the intake of lowest risk for women is about 3.4 g a day by Table 3 (5 in Table 2), and about 7.4 g for social-status-adjusted curves (9 in Table 2), where the curves are flat.
reporting_issues.consequence: The two maximum-protection values for study size appear transposed; the authors' conclusion of no difference by size (P = .61) is unaffected, but size-specific values should not be cited.

reporting_issues.issue: Two intervals in Table 2 are not compatible with their estimates on a symmetric (log) scale: not adjusted 36% (21 to 40), that is RR 0.64 (0.60 to 0.79), and follow-up over 10 years 15% (13 to 27), that is RR 0.85 (0.73 to 0.87); the row for all curves uses a 95% interval while every other row uses 99% (editors' arithmetic).
reporting_issues.consequence: Probably typographical (for example 31 to 40 and 13 to 17); these intervals should not be cited as printed.

reporting_issues.issue: In Figure 4D the dashed curve labelled 'Follow-up >10 y' is the deeper one (lowest RR about 0.78) with the wider interval, while Table 2, Table 3 and the text give greater protection with follow-up of 10 years or less (21% against 15%); the longer-follow-up group also has more deaths (61,532 against 25,409), which should give it the narrower interval.
reporting_issues.consequence: The figure legend appears swapped; the tables and text should be cited for the direction of the follow-up difference.

reporting_issues.issue: Counts in the text do not all match the tables: the text gives 28 European, 17 American and 11 other curves, while Table 1 and Table 2 (adjusted curves plus the 8 unadjusted European curves) imply 27, 16 and 13; Table 1 places Goldberg et al. (1994), whose reference title names the Honolulu Heart Program, under Japan, although Honolulu is in the United States; the adjustment codes in Table 1 give 27 curves adjusted for social class against 28 in Table 2; and Tolstrup et al. (2004) carry no age code although all adjusted curves are described as adjusted at least for age (editors' counts).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor for the pooled curve; the regional comparison in men may include two US curves in the 'Australia, Japan, China' group.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says the inverse association extended up to 4 drinks a day in men and 2 in women, and its conclusion names 2 to 4 drinks for men and 1 to 2 for women; the Results say up to 3 drinks a day in men and 2 in women, and Table 2's reversion points are 38 and 18 g a day. The drinks are 10-g drinks (figure axes), which the abstract does not say.
reporting_issues.consequence: Claims should use grams a day and the reversion points; in standard drinks of 14 g, 38 g is under 3 drinks (editors' conversion).

reporting_issues.issue: The subgroup without light or former drinkers in the reference group is described as using no alcohol intake with former drinkers excluded (Results › Other subgroup analyses), as excluding 'either ex-drinkers or very light drinkers' (Comment), and as 'No Drinkers in Reference Group' (Figure 4A legend).
reporting_issues.consequence: Whether occasional drinkers were excluded from the reference group in these 27 curves is unclear, so the 16% estimate may still carry some reference-group contamination.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 3's standard error for b1 in large studies, 0.0664, gives z of about 2.2, inconsistent with the printed P < .001 and four times the small-study value (0.0160) despite 16 times the participants; the P values for women in Europe and in other countries match one-sided rather than two-sided tests (for example b2 0.0295, SE 0.0149: two-sided P about .048, printed .02); and the women's regional P value is printed as > .54 while one Sidak-adjusted pairwise P is .53 (editors' arithmetic).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; signals transcription errors in the statistical tables, consistent with reporting issues 1 and 2.
